2026-11-22.title: Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe · Solemnity
readings: I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep
The Lord is my shepherd; there is nothing I shall want

Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me
2026-11-22.alt: Last Sunday of the liturgical year (34th Sunday in Ordinary Time). Next Sunday the new year begins with the First Sunday of Advent, Year B.
2026-11-22.verse: And the king will answer them, ‘Truly I tell you, just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me.’
theo: The Church year ends with a crown. Pope Pius XI instituted this solemnity in 1925 (Quas Primas), as nations were trying to organise life without God; since 1969 it closes the liturgical year, so that all history is seen moving toward Christ. But what kind of King is he? Ezekiel answers first: “I myself will search for my sheep… I myself will be the shepherd of my sheep.” God's kingship is shepherding: seeking the lost, binding up the injured, strengthening the weak.

The Gospel shows the same King at the end of time, seated on the throne of glory with all nations before him. The surprise is the standard of judgement. He does not ask about rank, wealth or even religious achievement, but about the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner: “just as you did it to one of the least of these… you did it to me.” Christ identifies himself with the poor. The Church draws from this the corporal works of mercy (CCC 2447) and teaches that we cannot be united with God unless we freely choose to love him, and we cannot love God if we fail to love our neighbour (CCC 1033).

Paul gives the cosmic scope: “Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who have died”; he must reign “until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” Then he hands the kingdom to the Father, “so that God may be all in all”. His reign is not imposed by force; it grows wherever love is chosen. Each act of mercy is a small coronation of Christ the King.
conn: Pius XI wrote Quas Primas after the First World War, as secularism and new totalitarian ideologies spread. Mexican martyrs under persecution died crying “¡Viva Cristo Rey!”, “Long live Christ the King!”
In Palestine sheep and goats grazed together by day but were often separated at night, as goats need more warmth. Every listener had seen a shepherd do it.
The six works in Matthew 25, plus burying the dead (Tobit 1:17–18), make the Church's seven corporal works of mercy.
Both the blessed and the cursed ask, “Lord, when was it that we saw you…?” Neither group knew whom they were serving or ignoring. Love is real when it does not calculate.

In the ancient Near East kings were called shepherds of their people. Ezekiel 34 condemns Israel's bad shepherd-kings; God himself will shepherd, and his servant David (the Messiah) will be prince among them (34:23–24).
1 Corinthians 15:28 is the Bible's widest horizon: history ends not in destruction but in God filling everything with his life.
altar: On the altar the King is present as he chose to reign: under the signs of bread broken and wine poured out. His throne is the Cross; his crown is thorns; his royal banquet is given to the poor in spirit.
Mother Teresa used to say that the Christ we receive in the Eucharist is the same Christ we touch in the poorest of the poor. From the altar we go to the least of his brothers and sisters.
outline: Ask: if Christ is King, where is his palace? Answer: in the hungry, the sick, the prisoner.
God himself seeks, gathers, heals and feeds his flock.
Point 2 · The King hidden in the least
At the end we will be asked only about love.
Point 3 · His Kingdom has no end
Christ reigns until death is destroyed and God is all in all.
The crown of thorns and the plate of rice given to a hungry man: both are Christ's throne.

term: Christ is King by nature as the Son of God and by right as Redeemer. His Kingdom is “not from this world” (John 18:36) but is present in mystery in the Church and will be completed in glory.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we end the Church year by crowning Christ as King. But what kind of King is he?

The prophet Ezekiel tells us: God says, “I myself will search for my sheep… I will seek the lost, bring back the strayed, bind up the injured, strengthen the weak.” Our King is a Shepherd. He does not rule by fear; he rules by care.

In the Gospel we see this King at the end of time, seated on his glorious throne, with all the nations before him. And what will he ask us? Not how much money we earned, not how many titles we held, not even how many devotions we attended. He will ask: “I was hungry, did you feed me? I was a stranger, did you welcome me? I was sick, did you visit me? I was in prison, did you come to me?”

And both groups are surprised: “Lord, when did we see you?” The King answers: “Just as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me.” Christ hides himself in the poor. St John Chrysostom said: do not honour Christ in church with silk while you neglect him outside, naked and cold.

St Paul tells us that Christ must reign until every enemy is defeated, and the last enemy is death. Then God will be all in all. That is where history is going. Every act of mercy, every plate of food shared, every visit to a lonely person, is a step in that direction: a small crowning of Christ.

So this last week of the year, let us choose one work of mercy each day. And when we say in the Our Father, “Thy Kingdom come,” let us mean it with our hands as well as our lips. Long live Christ the King!
kids: Children, what does a king wear? A crown! Jesus is our King, but his crown was made of thorns.

He is a King who looks after people like a shepherd looks after his sheep.
This week, help one person: share your snack, visit a sick grandparent, be kind to a new classmate. That's how we crown Jesus!

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, on this last Sunday of the liturgical year we proclaim Christ as King of the universe. We sing, we crown His image, we carry Him in procession. But let us remember what kind of crown He wore on earth: a crown of thorns.

When Pilate asked Jesus whether He was a king, Jesus answered: my kingdom is not from this world. He came to testify to the truth, and everyone who belongs to the truth listens to His voice (John 18:36–37). Pilate had soldiers, a palace and the power of Rome. Jesus had nothing but truth and love. Yet two thousand years later Pilate is remembered only because his name is in our Creed, and Jesus reigns in the hearts of millions.

Above the Cross the soldiers nailed an inscription: this is the King of the Jews (Luke 23:38). They meant it as a mockery, but it was the truth. Christ reigns from the Cross. His power is not to take life but to give it. And the first one to recognise His kingship was a dying criminal who said: Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. Jesus answered: today you will be with me in Paradise (Luke 23:42–43).

So the real question today is not whether Christ is King of the universe. He is, whether the world accepts it or not. The question is whether He is King of my heart. Does He reign over my tongue, my money, my phone, my family, my work, my politics? Or have I kept some area of my life closed to Him, a little kingdom of my own?

As we end this liturgical year, let us open every door to Christ. Let us serve as He served, especially the least of His brothers and sisters. And when we receive Him in this Holy Mass, let us say with the good thief: Jesus, remember me in your kingdom. That prayer is enough to save a whole life.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, this feast is younger than many of us think. Pope Pius XI established it in 1925, in the encyclical Quas Primas. Europe had just come out of a terrible war, ideologies were rising that put the State or the race in the place of God, and many nations were living as if God did not exist. The Pope proclaimed: Christ is King, of individuals, of families and of societies.

Why is Christ King? First, by His very nature: He is the eternal Son of God, through whom and for whom all things were created (Colossians 1:15–17). Second, by conquest: He redeemed us, not with silver or gold, but with His precious blood (1 Peter 1:18–19). Third, because the Father has given Him all authority in heaven and on earth (Matthew 28:18). Daniel saw one like a son of man receiving an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13–14).

His Kingdom is already present and not yet complete. The Second Vatican Council says that the Church is the Kingdom of Christ already present in mystery (Lumen Gentium 3). It grows quietly like a mustard seed. But it will be fulfilled only when Christ comes again in glory, when He hands over the Kingdom to the Father and God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:24–28; CCC 671). Until then we pray every day: Thy kingdom come.

Does this feast have anything to say to society? Yes. The Catechism teaches that Christians have the duty to bring the spirit of the Gospel into the life of society, its customs, laws and structures (CCC 2105). That means defending the dignity of every human life from conception to natural death, working for justice and peace, caring for the poor and the migrant. It does not mean forcing faith on anyone; the Church respects freedom of conscience. We propose Christ by our witness.

Through Baptism we share in Christ's royal office, which means to serve (CCC 786). The King washed feet. So let us end this liturgical year by renewing our allegiance to Christ, and let us show it by serving the least of His brothers and sisters. Then His Kingdom will come, a little more, in our homes and in our land.

intro: Christ the King reigns as Shepherd, is hidden in the least, and will reign until God is all in all.

sub: God himself seeks his scattered sheep.
He binds up and strengthens.
Jesus is the Good Shepherd who gives his life.
q: For thus says the Lord GOD: I myself will search for my sheep, and will seek them out. As shepherds seek out their flocks when they are among their scattered sheep, so I will seek out my sheep. I will rescue them from all the places to which they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness.
I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
points.apply: Seek out one person who has strayed from the parish.

q: As for you, my flock, thus says the Lord GOD: I shall judge between sheep and sheep, between rams and goats.

Then the king will say to those at his right hand, ‘Come, you that are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me something to drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me, I was naked and you gave me clothing, I was sick and you took care of me, I was in prison and you visited me.’

sub: Death is the last enemy.

q: To him was given dominion and glory and kingship, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him. His dominion is an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away, and his kingship is one that shall never be destroyed.

Then the seventh angel blew his trumpet, and there were loud voices in heaven, saying, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah, and he will reign forever and ever.”
